newsitem.title: USA: No problems before Texas plant blast - survivor.
newsitem.headline: No problems before Texas plant blast - survivor.

text.p: A worker who survived a plant explosion that killed eight of his colleagues this week said there was no indication of any problems before the blast.

Santiago Galindo told the Houston Chronicle in an interview published Thursday gauges on a pressurized tank that exploded showed the tank had been depressurized, as was normal procedure, and was safe to open up for maintenance.

In an with another worker at the Wyman-Gordon Co. metal forging plant, the newspaper said Wednesday that maintenance crews had neglected to check the gauges before opening the nitrogen-filled tank. Plant managers have said the 90-foot-tall tank, which builds up high pressure to drive powerful metal forging tools, apparently blew up when it was opened while still pressurized.
Wallace Whitney, spokesman for the North Grafton, Mass.-based Wyman-Gordon, told Reuters the company had not begun its own investigation into the blast and could not comment on the newspaper reports.
Eight men died in the explosion and two were injured, including Galindo, supervisor of the maintenance team.

"The gauges were reading zero. That's the first thing we checked (before opening the tanks)," Galindo, 57, told the Chronicle from his hospital bed. He said the crew was on top of the tank removing the bolts that held on its 8-inch thick steel lid when it blew off. "I never knew what hit me," he said.

Galindo, who lost an eye in the blast, said the men who died were directly over the lid, while he was standing a few feet away. He had just sent the other survivor, 31-year-old Gregory Dargin, on break. Dargin suffered only minor injuries.
The tank lid blew off with such force that it was found 150 yards away, investigators said.

Galindo's account contradicted Wednesday's report in which a worker from another maintenance team said the explosion occurred because no one checked to see if the tanks had been depressurized. "We just assumed (the pressure) was all let out. We just been doing it so long we just overlooked it," said the worker, who asked not to be identified.
